# Where flexibility gets trapped

Six hourly decisions: accept future energy deliveries / upward reserve and choose current battery dispatch. Firm promises narrow the feasible energy band. The default run reveals prices progressively; an optional condition announces exactly the next hour’s price. This is perfect hypothetical notice, not a market forecast. Offers still arrive at their original times.

`engine.js` is pure. Battery: 4 MW, 8 MWh, 4 MWh initial stock, 90% efficiency each direction. One net action per hour. Contract energy replaces spot settlement; standby reserve pays once, retains its discharge energy and removes its MW from import and export capacity. A backward energy floor preserves a path to honour future promises. Cash includes £2/grid MWh throughput cost. Net result adjusts final versus initial stock at £45/stored MWh.

Both policies use current-price thresholds: charge at ≤£45/MWh, export at ≥£85/MWh, otherwise hold, within feasibility. Firm accepts feasible offers in displayed order; Open declines all. With one-hour notice, both first charge if the announced price is ≥£85 and `next × 0.81 − current − 2 × (1 + 0.81) > 0`. This deliberately short-sighted preparation rule is not an optimiser. It considers neither later unseen prices nor an ideal dispatch across contracts. Only `publicView` supplies policy inputs; it exposes observed prices, declared next-hour notice, current offers and promises. Completed days show all four matched policy/information combinations and offer stepwise replays. Day 2 demonstrates a notice benefit for Open; day 14 changes neither policy.

`study.js` diagnoses requested dispatch and current offers against actual feasibility. It enumerates all smallest release sets among active visible promises, handling joint and alternative causes. The candidate offer cannot itself be released. Physical impossibility without other promises is distinguished from their effect. Labels trace each promise to its acceptance and delivery hour. The explorer fixes actual stock/time: hypothetical releases never mutate contracts, cash or earlier energy use. It is a local feasibility counterfactual, not cancellation pricing or a replay of history.

No forecast calibration, reserve activation, grid constraints, ramping, self-discharge or detailed degradation. Reserve power is conservatively unavailable even while charging. Same-export-at-spot changes settlement only; whole-run comparisons are needed for strategy opportunity cost. Terminal stock valuation is an accounting convention, not a physical sale. The chart shows physical feasibility, not a probability interval.

`thinking-lab:flexibility:v1` retains its key and decision-replay format, adding `conditions.priceNotice`. Old runs default to current-price-only and reproduce their results. Information stays fixed after the first hour. Changing it before then preserves staged manual choices; removing information already seen marks the run informed. Same-day manual replays are informed. Completed paths overlay only runs with matching price notice; saved-run tables label information and hindsight. Markdown includes conditions, matched results and an open diagnostic when exporting mid-run.

Run `node --test dist/flexibility/*.test.js`. Tests cover physical/cash conservation over 240 runs, reserve deliverability, future feasibility, reachable-band extremes, information boundaries, matched schedules, joint/alternative release sets, physical impossibility, legacy saves and policy counterexamples. Real browser journeys cover desktop/phone, touch and keyboard, persistence and downloads.

`window.flexibilityExperiment` exposes the same visible information and validated actions. Optional WebMCP tools read state and stage/commit an hour, detecting `document.modelContext` then a navigator fallback. Contract tests use a stub registry; native browser WebMCP remains unavailable in the test browser. No external requests or libraries.
